toc.title: Identities, the root user, policies and passwords

html:
1What You Will Learn

Note

Acronyms in this note. IAM: Identity and Access Management; KMS: Key Management Service; EC2: Elastic Compute Cloud; SAML: Security Assertion Markup Language; TLS: Transport Layer Security; SMS: Short Message Service; AD: Active Directory

  • Explain why the root user needs special care and name the tasks only it can do
  • Tell IAM users, groups and roles apart and say when each one fits
  • Read the parts of an IAM policy and apply least privilege
  • Choose among passwords, access keys, multi-factor authentication (MFA) and temporary credentials
  • Match Secrets Manager, Parameter Store, IAM Identity Center, Amazon Cognito and AWS Directory Service to the need

2Identities, the root user, policies and passwords

Running case

Tidewater's First AWS Account

  • Tidewater Outfitters has just opened its first AWS account, using the founder's email address
  • Five staff need the console, and a contractor must read one bucket of product photos
  • The shop's web servers read product images from storage, and a developer keeps keys in a shared file
  • Soon customers will sign in to a mobile app and upload photos of their gear
  • Your job: give each of them the right access, and nothing more

Authentication and Authorization: Two Questions

  • Authentication answers "who are you?": a password, a code from a device or a key proves it
  • Authorization answers "what may you do?": permissions written in policies decide
  • A principal is an identity that can send a request: the root user, an IAM user or an IAM role
  • AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) controls both, and adds no charge of its own
  • IAM changes are eventually consistent: a new user or policy can take a moment to take effect
Exam tip

"Who is signing in?" is authentication; "what is allowed?" is authorization.

The Root User: All Power, Few Uses

  • Every account begins with one sign-in identity, the root user, with complete access to every service and resource
  • You sign in with the email address and password used to create the account
  • You cannot attach identity-based policies to the root user or set a permissions boundary for it
  • In an AWS Organizations member account, the root user is still limited by service control policies
  • Use it only for the few tasks that need it
Exam tip

The root user is not an IAM user, and everyday work should never be done with it.

Protecting the Root User: Habits That Matter

  • Turn on MFA: AWS requires it for every root user, so register a device at first sign-in or within the grace period (14 days)
  • Use a strong, unique password, kept in a password manager
  • Do not create access keys for the root user; delete any that exist
  • Use a group email address that several people watch, not one person's inbox
  • Create an administrative identity for daily work; in AWS Organizations, remove root credentials from member accounts

Exam tip

For "how do you protect the root user?", think MFA, no access keys and no daily use.

Tasks Only the Root User Can Do [Verify live]

Group Tasks that need root credentials
The account itself change a standalone account's settings (email, root password, root access keys); close or reopen it; restore permissions after an administrator lock-out
Billing activate IAM access to the Billing and Cost Management console; some billing tasks and tax invoices
Storage and queues enable MFA delete on an S3 bucket; fix a policy that locks everyone out
Other register as a Reserved Instance Marketplace seller; sign up for AWS GovCloud (US); recover an unmanageable AWS KMS key
  • Older study lists also name changing the Support plan; the current IAM page does not
  • As of 4 November 2026: check the IAM page "Tasks that require root user credentials"
Exam tip

Account-level tasks and lock-outs need the root user; creating users or launching instances does not.

IAM Users, Groups and Roles

  • An IAM user is an identity with long-term credentials: a password and up to two access keys
  • An IAM group is a set of users that share permissions; it is not something that signs in
  • An IAM role has no long-term credentials: whoever assumes it receives temporary credentials
  • Use IAM users only where federation or roles cannot be used, such as certain third-party tools

Exam tip

Long-term credentials mean a user; temporary credentials mean a role.

IAM Groups: One Place for Shared Permissions

  • Attach an identity-based policy to a group, and every user in it receives the permissions
  • A group can hold many users, and a user can belong to several groups
  • Groups cannot be nested: they hold users only, never other groups
  • There is no default group that contains every user; you create one and add users yourself
  • A group cannot be a principal in a policy, because groups carry permissions, not sign-in identity
  • Tidewater tip: when someone changes jobs, move them between groups instead of editing their permissions
Exam tip

Groups simplify permissions for users; they do not sign in and cannot contain groups.

IAM Roles and Temporary Credentials

  • A role is an identity with permissions, meant to be assumed by anyone or anything that needs it
  • Assuming a role returns temporary security credentials for that session
  • Who can assume a role: IAM users, other roles, AWS services such as Amazon EC2 and AWS Lambda, and federated people
  • AWS delivers the role's credentials to the instance or function, so no keys are stored
  • Some services create service-linked roles, tied to that service, which assumes them for you

Exam tip

For an application on AWS that needs access, the answer is a role, not stored keys.

Cross-Account Access and Federation

  • A role in your account can be assumed by a user in another account, which is how access is shared across accounts
  • Two policies work together: the trust policy says who may assume the role, and the permissions policy says what they may do
  • Federation lets people use an identity from an outside provider (SAML 2.0, the Security Assertion Markup Language, or OpenID Connect) and receive a role with temporary credentials
  • AWS recommends federation for human users, so people do not need long-term IAM users

Exam tip

Cross-account access and federation both end the same way: a role and temporary credentials.

Reading an IAM Policy

  • A policy is a document (usually JSON) made of one or more statements
  • Effect: Allow or Deny
  • Action: what can be done, such as reading an object
  • Resource: what it can be done to, such as one bucket
  • Condition (optional): when it applies, such as only with MFA or only over TLS
  • Principal: who is allowed, shown only in resource-based policies
  • An explicit Deny always wins over an Allow

Exam tip

You do not need to write JSON, but you do need to know what Effect, Action, Resource and Condition do.

Policy Types: Identity-Based and Resource-Based

Type Attached to Notes
Identity-based a user, group or role AWS managed (created by AWS), customer managed (created by you), or inline (one identity only)
Resource-based a resource Names the principal; examples: an Amazon S3 bucket policy and a role's trust policy
  • AWS managed policies are a good start but are written for everyone, so they may grant more than you need
  • Customer managed policies give precise control and can be reused across identities
  • Inline policies live and die with one identity
Exam tip

A policy on a bucket that names who may read it is resource-based.

Guardrails Limit; Policies Grant Beyond the guide

  • A permissions boundary sets the maximum an identity-based policy can give one user or role
  • A service control policy (SCP) in AWS Organizations sets the maximum for accounts, including each account's root user
  • Neither one grants anything: an identity or resource policy must still allow the action
  • When policies conflict, an explicit Deny in any of them overrides every Allow
  • Tidewater tip: think of guardrails as the fence and policies as the gates inside it
Exam tip

If a question says the policy "limits" or "caps" permissions, it is a boundary or an SCP, not a grant.

Least Privilege in Practice

  • Least privilege means giving only the permissions a task needs, on the resources it needs, under the conditions that fit
  • Start with an AWS managed policy if you must, then narrow it with a customer managed policy
  • IAM Access Analyzer can generate a policy from the activity recorded in AWS CloudTrail
  • Last accessed information shows permissions that are never used, so you can remove them
  • Review and remove unused users, roles, permissions and credentials regularly
  • Add conditions, for example to require MFA or TLS
Exam tip

When two answers both work, choose the one that grants fewer permissions.

Passwords and Access Keys [Verify live]

  • Default password policy: 8 to 128 characters, three of four character types, not the account name or email; passwords never expire
  • Custom policy: length 6 to 128, expiry 1 to 1,095 days, reuse prevention of 1 to 24 passwords
  • It does not cover the root user or access keys, and there is no lockout setting
  • Access keys are an ID plus a secret; a user can have two; the secret shows only at creation
  • Never put keys in code, and never create them for the root user
  • As of 4 November 2026: values are from the IAM User Guide
Exam tip

Prefer roles to keys; if keys must exist, rotate them and delete the unused ones.

3MFA, secrets, directories and practice

Multi-Factor Authentication [Verify live]

  • MFA adds a second factor to the sign-in: something you have, in addition to the password
  • Passkeys and security keys use public key cryptography and resist phishing; AWS recommends them first
  • Virtual authenticator apps on a phone make time-based one-time passwords (TOTP)
  • Hardware TOTP tokens show a six-digit code
  • SMS text message MFA is no longer supported
  • The root user and each IAM user can register up to eight MFA devices; one is enough to sign in
  • As of 4 November 2026: supported types are listed in the IAM User Guide

Exam tip

MFA is "something you know plus something you have"; passkeys and security keys resist phishing best.

Where to Keep Secrets: Secrets Manager and Parameter Store

  • AWS Secrets Manager stores and retrieves secrets such as database credentials, API keys and tokens, and can rotate them automatically
  • Applications fetch the secret at run time, so no hard-coded credentials sit in the code
  • Secrets are encrypted with AWS KMS, and access is controlled with IAM
  • AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store holds configuration values, such as endpoints and approved image IDs; its SecureString type encrypts a value with KMS
  • Parameter Store does not rotate credentials; AWS points to Secrets Manager for passwords and keys
Exam tip

Credentials that must rotate: Secrets Manager. Plain settings: Parameter Store.

IAM Identity Center: One Front Door for Your Workforce Old name

  • AWS IAM Identity Center gives workforce users single sign-on to many AWS accounts and to AWS applications
  • Manage people in its own directory, or connect an existing identity provider
  • A permission set is a template of policies; assigning it creates roles in each target account
  • Users reach everything through the AWS access portal, with MFA available
  • Best practice is an organization instance in the AWS Organizations management account
  • It was called AWS Single Sign-On before it was renamed, and older material still uses that name

Exam tip

For workforce single sign-on across many accounts, choose IAM Identity Center.

Amazon Cognito and AWS Directory Service

  • Amazon Cognito is for your application's customers
  • A user pool is a user directory that signs people in and issues tokens, including through Google or Apple
  • An identity pool swaps a trusted sign-in for temporary AWS credentials
  • AWS Directory Service is for Microsoft Active Directory: AWS Managed Microsoft AD is a real directory in AWS, AD Connector forwards sign-ins to your on-premises directory, Simple AD is a small compatible directory

Exam tip

Customers of your app: Cognito. Windows and Active Directory needs: Directory Service.

What the Exam Asks: Identity and Access

  • User or role: long-term credentials or temporary ones
  • Group or role: shared permissions for users, or an identity you assume
  • Identity-based or resource-based: attached to who, or to what
  • Limit or grant: guardrails cap, policies allow
  • Secrets Manager or Parameter Store: rotating credentials or plain configuration
  • Identity Center or Cognito: your workforce, or your app's customers
  • Managed AD, AD Connector or Simple AD: a real directory, a pass-through, or a small one
Exam tip

Name the need first, then the service.

Design Check: Tidewater's Access Plan

Tidewater's need Choose
The founder's account-owner sign-in Root user with MFA, locked away, used only for root-only tasks
Five staff in the console IAM Identity Center users and permission sets, not shared logins
A contractor reading one bucket A role (or permission set) allowing read on that bucket only, for a limited time
Web servers reading photos A role for the EC2 instances, no keys
A developer's shared key file Delete the keys; use a role, or Secrets Manager for a credential that must exist
Customers on the mobile app Cognito user pool plus identity pool
  • Cover the right column, answer each row yourself, then compare

Try It: Least Privilege in Twenty Minutes (Optional)

  • Goal: see least privilege work in a practice account; IAM costs nothing
  • Start: sign in as an administrator, not as the root user
  • Create a group named ReadOnlyPhotos and attach a customer managed policy that allows only reading objects in one test bucket
  • Add a test user to the group, sign in as that user, read an object, then try to delete one and see it fail
  • Review the Access Advisor tab for the user; then clean up the user, group, policy and bucket

Lists the policies attached to the group (the group name is an example)

aws iam list-attached-group-policies --group-name ReadOnlyPhotos
Exam tip

Hands-on work is not tested on this exam; it helps the ideas stay in your head.

4Exam Q&A

4.1 Practice questions (choose the best answer; some ask for two)

S1Which AWS identity is created with the account, has complete access to everything in it, and should be used only for the few tasks that require it?

  • AAn IAM role assumed by the account owner
  • BAn IAM user in an Administrators group
  • CThe AWS account root user
  • DAn IAM Identity Center administrator
Show the answer

Answer: C. Every account starts with the root user, which signs in with the email address and password used at sign-up and has complete access. An IAM user, a role or an Identity Center administrator is created later and can be limited, so none of them is the account's original identity.

S2Which task requires you to sign in as the root user?

  • ACreate an IAM group and add the finance team to it
  • BAttach an AWS managed policy to an existing IAM role
  • CLaunch an Amazon EC2 instance in a chosen Region
  • DRestore access after the only IAM administrator removed their own permissions
Show the answer

Answer: D. Restoring permissions when the only IAM administrator has locked themselves out is on the list of tasks that need root credentials. Creating groups, attaching policies and launching instances are everyday tasks that an administrative identity can perform.

S3Tidewater's founder signed up with a personal email. Which TWO actions best protect the root user? (Select TWO.)

  • ACreate root access keys so that scripts can run with full access
  • BRegister MFA for the root user, preferably a passkey or security key
  • CUse the root user for everyday administration to keep identities few
  • DShare the root password with the shop manager for emergencies
  • ECreate an administrative identity for daily work and keep root for root-only tasks
Show the answer

Answer: B, E. MFA protects the sign-in, and an administrative identity keeps the root user out of daily use. Root access keys, daily use of the root user and sharing its password all widen the exposure of the most powerful identity in the account.

S4Tidewater's web servers on Amazon EC2 must read product photos from an Amazon S3 bucket. What is the best way to grant that access?

  • AAttach an IAM role with the needed S3 permissions to the instances
  • BStore an IAM user's access keys in a configuration file on each server
  • CCreate access keys for the root user and load them at startup
  • DGive the bucket a public policy so that no credentials are needed
Show the answer

Answer: A. A role delivers temporary credentials to the instances automatically, so no long-term keys are stored. Keys in a file can leak, root keys give far too much power, and a public policy would expose the photos to everyone.

S5A policy attached to an Amazon S3 bucket that names which principals may read its objects is an example of which policy type?

  • AA permissions boundary
  • BA service control policy
  • CA resource-based policy
  • DAn inline identity-based policy
Show the answer

Answer: C. A policy attached to a resource that names the principals allowed to use it is resource-based; a bucket policy is the usual example. Boundaries and service control policies only limit permissions, and an identity-based policy is attached to a user, group or role.

S6A developer must read objects in one S3 bucket and nothing else. Which approach best follows the principle of least privilege?

  • AAttach the AdministratorAccess managed policy so the developer is never blocked
  • BCreate a customer managed policy that allows only reading objects in that bucket
  • CAttach the AmazonS3FullAccess managed policy for every bucket in the account
  • DShare the credentials of an administrator who already has access
Show the answer

Answer: B. Least privilege grants only the actions the task needs on only the resources it needs, which a narrow customer managed policy does. Administrator access, full S3 access and shared administrator credentials all give far more than the task requires.

S7Which TWO are MFA options that AWS supports for IAM users? (Select TWO.)

  • AA passkey or security key
  • BA code sent by SMS text message
  • CA security question answered at sign-in
  • DA virtual authenticator app that generates one-time codes
  • EA code sent to the user's email address
Show the answer

Answer: A, D. AWS supports passkeys and security keys, virtual authenticator apps and hardware TOTP tokens. AWS has ended support for enabling SMS text message MFA, and security questions and email codes are not MFA options for IAM.

S8Tidewater's mobile app lets customers sign up with an email address or a Google account, and then upload photos to Amazon S3 with limited permissions. Which combination meets this need?

  • AIAM users created for each customer, with access keys stored in the app
  • BIAM Identity Center users with a permission set that allows S3 access
  • CAWS Directory Service for Microsoft Active Directory with a trust relationship
  • DAn Amazon Cognito user pool for sign-in and an identity pool for temporary AWS credentials
Show the answer

Answer: D. A Cognito user pool signs customers in, including through Google, and an identity pool exchanges that sign-in for temporary, limited AWS credentials. Per-customer IAM users with stored keys do not scale, Identity Center is for your workforce, and Directory Service is for Active Directory needs.

5Quick Reference Card

Topic Key fact
Root user complete access; use MFA, no access keys and no daily use; only a short list of tasks needs it
Identities users have long-term credentials, groups share permissions, roles give temporary credentials
Policies identity-based and resource-based policies grant; boundaries and SCPs only limit; an explicit deny wins
Least privilege start small, use Access Analyzer and last accessed information, add conditions
Credentials password policy, two access keys per user, MFA with passkeys, apps or hardware tokens, and no SMS
Services Secrets Manager for secrets, Parameter Store for settings, Identity Center for the workforce, Cognito for app customers, Directory Service for Active Directory
